render.title: How cytoplasmic NADH electrons enter the mitochondrion via shuttle systems
render.body:
You are right that NADH itself cannot cross the inner mitochondrial membrane — the membrane is impermeable to it. Cells solve this problem with indirect transfer systems called metabolic shuttles. The most important one in most tissues is the malate-aspartate shuttle.

Here is how the malate-aspartate shuttle works. In the cytoplasm, the enzyme malate dehydrogenase uses the electrons from NADH to reduce oxaloacetate to malate — this step re-oxidises the NADH to NAD+. Malate can cross the inner membrane through a specific transporter (the malate-alpha-ketoglutarate carrier). Once inside the matrix, a mitochondrial malate dehydrogenase re-oxidises malate back to oxaloacetate, this time donating the electrons to NAD+ inside the matrix to make mitochondrial NADH. That mitochondrial NADH can then donate electrons at Complex I, just as if the original NADH had crossed the membrane.

To keep the cycle going, the oxaloacetate produced inside the matrix cannot cross the inner membrane directly either. It is transaminated to aspartate, which does have a transporter (the aspartate-glutamate carrier). Aspartate exits to the cytoplasm, is converted back to oxaloacetate, and the cycle continues.

The net outcome is a one-for-one transfer of reducing equivalents: each cytoplasmic NADH consumed yields one mitochondrial NADH, so the full 2.5 ATP per NADH can still be produced by oxidative phosphorylation.

A second, simpler shuttle also exists: the glycerol-3-phosphate shuttle. In this system, cytoplasmic NADH reduces dihydroxyacetone phosphate to glycerol-3-phosphate, which crosses the outer membrane and is re-oxidised by a mitochondrial glycerol-3-phosphate dehydrogenase on the outer face of the inner membrane. However, this enzyme donates electrons to ubiquinone (CoQ) rather than to NAD+, entering the chain at Complex II level. The result is only about 1.5 ATP per cytoplasmic NADH — slightly less efficient than the malate-aspartate route. This shuttle is more prominent in muscle and brain.
render.summary: Cytoplasmic NADH cannot cross the inner mitochondrial membrane, so cells use metabolic shuttles. The malate-aspartate shuttle transfers reducing equivalents as malate into the matrix, where they regenerate mitochondrial NADH for Complex I — yielding the same ATP as if NADH had crossed directly. The glycerol-3-phosphate shuttle offers a simpler but slightly less efficient alternative, donating electrons to CoQ instead.
